steps.title: Find your change, read across the row
steps.body:
Each row starts with what you want to change and reads left to right: the file to edit, how to edit it, the command to re-run, and the part of the board that is rewritten.

The colours group the changes: green for the kernel, purple for the device tree, root filesystem and account, blue for UEFI, orange for your own carrier board.

steps.title: Kernel options and source changes both end in ./build.sh kernel
steps.body:
A kernel option is one line such as `CONFIG_FOO=y` in `config/kernel/my.cfg`, applied on top of the default kernel configuration. A driver or kernel source change is a file `patches/source/0001-….patch`, applied with `patch -p1` relative to `build/work/Linux_for_Tegra/source`.

Both run `./build.sh kernel`, and the result in `kernel/Image` and the modules lands in the `kernel` partition and in `APP`.

steps.title: A device tree change is a patch too, but lands elsewhere
steps.body:
Device tree edits are patches to files under `source/hardware/nvidia/t23x/nv-public/…`, built by `./build.sh kernel`. The device tree is the data file that tells the kernel what hardware exists.

The output is `kernel/dtb/*.dtb`, which goes to the `kernel-dtb` partition only, not to the root filesystem.

steps.title: Choosing the DTB is an extlinux.conf edit
steps.body:
To make the kernel boot with a different device tree, add an `FDT /boot/….dtb` line to `rootfs/boot/extlinux/extlinux.conf`. NVIDIA calls this 'DTB Support'.

Run `./build.sh image`. The change lands in `APP:/boot/extlinux/`, in the root filesystem.

steps.title: UEFI boot order changes the firmware flash
steps.body:
Boot order and boot mode are set with config variables (`ROOT_DEVICE`, `BOOT_ORDER_OVERLAY`) or by editing `kernel/dtb/L4TConfiguration.dtbo`, converting with `dtc -I dtb -O dts` and back.

This is the one row that needs `./build.sh image` and `./build.sh flash`, because UEFI variables live in QSPI-NOR, so the board must be in recovery mode again.

steps.title: Hostname, user and password live in local.conf
steps.body:
Set `TARGET_HOSTNAME`, `TARGET_USER` and `TARGET_PASSWORD` in `config/local.conf`, then run `clean`, `rootfs` and `image` so the account is created again.

The result is files under `rootfs/etc/…`, written into the `APP` partition.

steps.title: Packages and files go into rootfs/ as root
steps.body:
Edit the tree at `build/work/Linux_for_Tegra/rootfs/` with `sudo chroot` (using qemu to run arm64 binaries on the x86-64 PC) or copy files in as root, because the tree's files are owned by root.

Then `./build.sh image` packs it into the `APP` root filesystem.

steps.title: Your own carrier board means new boot firmware
steps.body:
Pinmux and pad voltage settings are read by MB1, so they live in its BCT. Copy the board `.conf` and edit `bootloader/generic/BCT/*.dtsi` for a new `BOARD` name and a new MB1-BCT (see docs/08 section 6).

Run `BOARD=… ./build.sh image && flash`. The change lands in QSPI-NOR, in both the A and B boot firmware.

steps.title: For kernel work, skip the flash
steps.body:
In the default boot mode the kernel comes from the root filesystem (`/boot/Image`, selected by `/boot/extlinux/extlinux.conf`).

So on a running board you can `scp` the new Image and modules, keep the old kernel as a second extlinux entry and reboot. No recovery mode is needed, and the old entry is your way back.

steps.title: Anything that touches boot firmware needs recovery mode
steps.body:
A change that lands in 'boot firmware' rewrites the QSPI-NOR flash, which needs recovery mode again. Rows that land in the kernel, DTB or `APP` leave the firmware alone.

Exact commands for every row are in `docs/08-customizing.md`.
